newsitem.title: FRANCE: French gvt set to tackle revenue side of 98 budget.
newsitem.headline: French gvt set to tackle revenue side of 98 budget.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was expected to tackle the revenue side of the 1998 finance act this week in the second leg of a budget crucial to France's preparations for European monetary union.

Economists said that even if the government managed to limit spending, it would have to find about 50 billion francs ($8.2 billion) of revenue to bring France's public deficits down to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) as required to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Jospin set the spending side of the budget on August 8 but released no details of his decisions. Government sources and newspaper reports have suggested spending will rise no more than the pace of economic growth but no less than inflation. The finance ministry has said spending will rise less than nominal GDP growth.
Economists expect inflation to rise between 1.2 and 1.6 percent next year while gross domestic product could climb by about 2.8 percent, compared to about two percent this year.
The budget will be presented to the cabinet on September 24.
France's Communist Party waded into the debate over the budget with a 100 billion franc programme to promote growth in the economy.

The Communist plan, which is still in the development stage includes taxing capital flows, a mandatory loan to the government from banks and insurance companies to pay the country's debt service, financial aid to local authorities so they can create jobs, higher employer charges and higher income taxes for the wealthiest.
But it also includes proposals for cutting income tax for all but the wealthiest families, lowering sales tax on essential items and cutting electricity, housing and other taxes.
The Communists said their programme would produce about 100 billion francs in new receipts to help relaunch the economy. The party's budget proposals are unlikely to enter the final 1998 finance act.
The government is depending on an increase in economic growth to help reverse the trend of lower tax receipts which has cut into its revenues.
But a pickup in growth, which is expected to help, will not be enough, economists said.
"The assumption that growth will be higher because of higher exports is not enough in my view," said Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris.

He predicted the economy would expand by 2.5 percent next year, but even if growth came in at 2.8 percent, the previous government's prediction, there would still be a revenue shortfall if there were no pickup in the domestic economy.

If domestic demand were to grow by 3.0 to 3.5 percent nominally as some economists predicted, that would produce about 25 billion francs of extra revenue, said Joanne Perez, economist at Merrill Lynch in Paris.
But Perez said this upturn was not a foregone conclusion as corporate tax increases and high social charges remained a strong disincentive for companies to invest in France.
Even with growth at the upper end of expectations, economists said they expected the government to resort to several one-time payments from public companies to fill the revenue gap.
The previous conservative government used a 37.5 billion franc payment in 1997 from state-owned telephone operator France Telecom to cut its deficit for the year.

The most likely candidate for a big contribution is utility Electricite de France (EdF). While the government has denied speculation in newspapers that it would take a levy on provisions in EdF's accounts, economists said they believed the government would find a way to tap the profitable state entity.
Newspapers have speculated that the government will restructure EdF to make it subject to higher taxes, and that it will take money from other state owned companies.

The government is reportedly studying cancelling income tax cuts planned for next year that were voted by the previous government. The measure would reinstate about 12 billion francs of revenue, but is seen as politically difficult due to its unpopularity.
Economists also expect the government to enact several tax changes to boost income.

During the parliamentary election campaign, the Socialists said they would consider shifting welfare payroll charges onto a wider and higher CSG tax, a levy on almost all income, to deal with continued shortfalls in the financing of France's heavily indebted welfare system.
